The presence of normal overall immunoglobulin levels with deficiency of specific immunoglobulins directed against bacterial polysaccharides.
Generalised myoclonic seizure provoked by flashing or flickering light.
Abnormal eating habits involve excessive or insufficient consumption of food, or any other abnormal pattern of food consumption.
Generalized-onset tonic-clonic seizures that are provoked by flashing or flickering light.
Sudden, repetitive, nonrhythmic motor movements (spasms), involving the eyes and muscles of the face.
A seizure characterized by a sensation in the head such as light-headedness or headache as its first clinical manifestation.

There is inconclusive evidence to precisely define the duration of the seizure; however, based on current evidence an operational threshold of 10 minutes is appropriate as beyond this a seizure is likely to be more prolonged. The individual may or may not be aware or in coma.

Epileptiform activity refers to distinctive EEG waves or complexes distinguished from background activity found in in a proportion of human subjects with epilepsy, but which can also be found in subjects without seizures. Interictal epileptiform activity refers to such activity that occurs in the absence of a clinical or subclinical seizure.

Generalized clonic seizure is a type of generalized motor seizure characterised by sustained bilateral jerking, either symmetric or asymmetric, that is regularly repetitive and involves the same muscle groups.
Abnormal function of the left ventricule during left ventricular relaxation and filling.
An increase in cell size, enhanced protein synthesis, and heightened organization of the sarcomere within cardiac myocytes.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with an symmetrical and concentric pattern of hypertrophy.
Diffuse thickening of the ventricular endocardium and by associated myocardial dysfunction
The presence of an abnormally short lingual frenulum.
Recurrent episodes of apnea occurring during infancy.
A developmental defect of pulmonary lobation characterized by the presence of only two lobes of the right lung.
Aplasia (absence) of the urinary bladder.
Yellow, white or greyish lesions in the retina that are well-defined/distinct, individual and mostly uniform in size.
A polar cataract that affects the anterior pole of the lens.

Abnormal function of the renal tubule. The basic functional unit of the kidney, the nephron, consists of a renal corpuscle attached to a renal tubule, with roughly 0.8 to 1.5 nephrons per adult kidney. The functions of the renal tubule include reabsorption of water, electrolytes, glucose, and amino acids and secretion of substances such as uric acid.
Aplasia (absence) of the distal phalanges.

Ambulation or other complex motor behaviors may occur after getting out of bed in a sleep-like state. During sleepwalking episodes, the individual who is somnambulating appears confused or dazed, with their eyes usually open. They may mumble or give inappropriate answers to questions, and occasionally appear agitated.
A parasomnia that occurs during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
A pattern of thinking and perceiving characterized by a loss of contact with reality, leading to significant changes in thoughts, perceptions, and behaviors.
Seizures that occur while the affected individual is sleeping.

A focal seizure characterized at onset by predominantly proximal limb or axial muscles producing irregular sequential ballistic movements, such as pedaling, pelvic thrusting, thrashing, rocking movements.
An autonomic seizure is a type of focal non-motor seizure characterized by alteration of autonomic nervous system function as the initial semiological feature.
Inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal (EAC), the auricle, or both.
A reduced ability of a T cell population to expand by cell division following T cell activation.
Absence of sex glands (gonads are the organs that produce gametes; testis in males and ovary in females).
An abnormality of the male internal genitalia.
A reduction below the normal range of the antimullerian hormone in the circulation.
Absence or underdevelopment of the testes.
A flattened vertebral body shape with reduced distance between the vertebral endplates affecting the cervical spine.
A noninflammatory, progressive occlusion of the intracranial carotid arteries owing to the formation of netlike collateral arteries arising from the circle of Willis.
Spasticity of one or more muscles innervated by the facial nerve.
A form of torticollis in which the head is drawn back, either due to a permanent contractures of neck extensor muscles, or to a spasmodic contracture.
Individuals with Pseudobulbar signs often also demonstrate abnormal behavioral symptoms such as inappropriate emotional outbursts of uncontrolled laughter or weeping etc.

A limitation in the passive range of motion of a joint of the lower limb resulting from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues owing to structural changes of non-bony tissues, such as muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules or skin.

A limitation in the passive range of motion of a joint of the upper limb resulting from loss of elasticity in the periarticular tissues owing to structural changes of non-bony tissues, such as muscles, tendons, ligaments, joint capsules or skin.
A segmental pattern of demyelination and regeneration (remyelination) affecting peripheral nerves.
The presence of multiple sausage-shaped swellings of the myelin sheath (The Latin tomaculum means sausage).
Involuntary flexion or extension of the arms and legs.
A reduction in immunoglobulin levels of the IgG2 subclass in the blood circulation.
The presence of a cleft in the cerebral cortex unilaterally or bilaterally, usually located in the frontal area.
Cleft palate of the midline of the palate.
Abnormality of the thymus, an organ located in the upper anterior portion of the chest cavity just behind the sternum and whose main function is to provide an environment for T lymphocyte maturation.
Location of the urethral opening on the inferior aspect of the penis.
Inability to react to a delayed hypersensitivity skin test.
Decreased or impaired activation of T cells in response to a mitogen, cytokine, chemokine, cellular ligand, or an antigen for which it is specific.
Absense of the central pair of microtubules in the sperm axoneme, thereby forming a 9+0 pattern instead of the normal 9+2 pattern.
Underdevelopment of the iliac bones.

A type of glomerular subepithelial deposit characterized by finely granular material deposited between the outer (epithelial) aspect of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and the visceral epithelial cell, with varying degrees of incorporation into the GBM and corresponding to immunoglobulin and/or complement by immunofluorescence/immunohistochemistry. This feature is associated with a prominent GBM reflecting an diffuse and relativly uniform increase in thickness (subjective estimate).
Duplicated basement membranes of the peritubular capillaries located in the medulla of the kidney and arranged in multiple concentric layers.
Sperm cells lacking flagella.
Sperm cells with abnormally short flagella.
Sperm cells whose flagella are twisted (coiled).
Increased diameter (caliber) of intrahepatic bile ducts (bile ducts that transport bile between the Canals of Hering and the interlobar bile ducts).

Obliteration of the glomerular capillary lumen by increased collagenous matrix, with or without hyalinosis or foam cells. Sclerosis involves 100% of the glomerular tuft. Relative to other patent glomeruli in the sample, glomerular size is preserved, or increased/decreased by no more than 50%.
Irregular or changing caliber (diameter) along the tail of the sperm.
Increased width of phalanx of one or more toes.
Increased width of the diaphysis of long bones.
Nail that appears thick when viewed on end.
Increased susceptibility to infections due to aspiration, as manifested by recurrent episodes of infections due to aspiration.
Lack of measurable response to stimulation of auditory evoked potentials.
A function abnormality of the endocrine pancreas.
An abnormality of the homeostasis (concentration) of iron cation.
A condition in which the affected individual cannot extend the wrist, which hangs flaccidly.
Reduced grip strength. Gripping is the motion by which the hand tightly grasps an object or other hand.
Muscular atrophy of distal arm muscles.
Reduced ability of the natural killer cell to function in the adaptive immune response.
Abnormal accumulation of fluid and swelling of the stroma of cornea.
A reduction in the thickness of Descemet's membrane.
A reduction in visual acuity with best corrected visual acuity between 1.40 (20/500) and 1.89 logMAR (up to roughly 20/1590).
An increase in the degree of curvature of the cornea compared to normal.
A reduction in the number of corneal endothelial cells.
Abnormality of Descemet's membrane, which is the basement membrane of the corneal endothelium.
Adhesions between the iris and the cornea.

This corneal dystrophy affects the posterior limiting membrane of the cornea and is characterized by polymorphous plaques of calcium deposits in the deep stromal layers of the cornea, and occasionally by vesicular lesions of the endothelium and edema of the deep corneal stroma.
The presence of an abnormal shape of the palpebral fissure.
A condition characterized by intermittent involuntary contraction of muscles (spasms) related to hypocalcemia or occasionally magnesium deficiency.
The LV end-diastolic internal diameter was measured from two-dimensional (2D) images in the parasternal long-axis view, timed with mitral valve closure at the level of the mitral valve chordae.
Passage of an increased number of stools containing mucus, a thick fluid substance secreted by mucous membranes.
Developmental hypoplasia (shortening) of middle phalanx of toe.
Decreased length of the tubular bones of the hand, that is, the phalanges and metacarpals.
Difficulty in performing one or more activities normally performed every day, such as eating, bathing, dressing, grooming, work, homemaking, and leisure.
An abnormally flattened femoral head.
A decreased ability to move the femur at the hip joint associated with a decreased range of motion of the hip.
Abnormal shortening of all middle phalanges of toes.
Flaring (increase of width with a splayed appearance) of the humeral metaphysis.
A type of disproportionate short stature characterized by a short trunk but a average-sized limbs with onset in childhood.
Muscular atrophy that does not display a progression in severity with time.
Progressive muscular atrophy affecting muscles in the distal portions of the extremities.
An abnormality of the process of endochondral ossification, which is a type of replacement ossification in which bone tissue replaces cartilage.
Excessive amounts of mucopolysaccharide in the urine.
Congenital lack of development of the muscles, which are then replaced by a mixture of dense fat and fibrous tissue.
Atrophy of the muscles that are responsible for moving the scapula, which are the levator scapulae, the infraspinatus muscle, the teres major, the teres minor, and the supraspinatus muscle.
Increase in size of one or more joints.

A developmental defect in a the clavicule leading to bending and pathologic fracture, with inability to form a normal bony callus with subsequent fibrous nonunion, leading to the pseudarthrosis (or false joint).
A decrease in the strength of the diaphragm.
An abnormality of the acetabulum, i.e., the Acetabular part of hip bone, which together with the head of the femur forms the hip joint.

The sacroiliac joint in the bony pelvis connects the sacrum and the ilium of the pelvis, which are joined by strong ligaments. The notch is located directly superior to the joint. This term refers to a reduction in the height of the notch.
The presence of wide, concave anterior rib ends.
Wide, concave rib end.
Absence of one or more epiphyses of the phalanges of the fingers.
Increased top to bottom height of vertebral bodies.
Disproportionately short middle and distal phalanges compared to the hand/foot.
The presence of a tail-like skin appendage located adjacent to the sacrum.

An anomalous radiographic appearance of the developing pelvis, in which the greater ischiadic noth (incisura ischiadica major) is shallow and the pelvis takes on the appearance said to resemble a halberd (a weapon especially of the 15th and 16th centuries consisting typically of a battle-ax and pike mounted on a handle).
The femur is shortened and displays flaring (widening) of the metaphyses.
Irregular surface of the normally relatively smooth capital femoral epiphysis.
A rounded, bulging chest that resembles the shape of a barrel. That is, there is an increased anteroposterior diameter and usually some degree of kyphosis.
Abnormally increased variability of the size of the vertebral bodies.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the groin region.
A bending or abnormal curvature of the radius.
An increase in the vertical distance between adjacent vertebral bodies, observed as an increase in the intervertebral disc space.
An abnormal flattening of an epiphysis of femur.
Short distance from the end of the toe to the most distal interphalangeal crease or distal interphalangeal joint flexion point, i.e., abnormally short distal phalanx of toe.
Exaggerated skin markings (dermatoglyphics) on the palms of the hand.
An abnormally reduced count of basophils per volume in the blood circulation.
An abnormally decreased level of immunoglobulin E (IgE) in blood.

A reduction in the normal proportion of memory B cells (CD19+/CD27+) in circulation relative to the total number of B cells. Memory B cells develop from naive B cells. Upon antigen rechallenge, memory B cells rapidly expand and differentiate into plasma cells under the cognate control of memory Th cells (Phase IV).
The presence of an abnormal membrane obstructing the urethra.
Obstruction of the flow of urine through the urethra.
A nonprogressive (i.e., stationary) form of difficulties with night blindness with congenital onset.
An abnormal reduction in the amplitude of the a-wave.

A dark-adapted bright flash electroretinogram in which the b-wave that is of markedly lower amplitude than the associated a-wave (source: Holder GE., Inherited Chorioretinal Dystrophies: A Textbook and Atlas; 2014; p.17; ISBN 978-3-540-69466-3).
A compensatory head posture occurs when the head is deviated out of the normal primary straight head position in order to compensate for an ocular problem.

A type of astigmatism in which an unequal curvature of the cornea and some cases additionally of the lens causes one meridian of the eye to be hyperopic (farsighted) and a second meridian that is perpendicular to the first to be myopic (nearsighted).
Absence of the nasal bone.
Pain or discomfort of the scalp elicited by palpation.
Presence of more than one exostosis. An exostosis is a benign growth the projects outward from the bone surface. It is capped by cartilage, and arises from a bone that develops from cartilage.
Visually assessable vertical indentation, cleft, or depression of the nasal bridge, ridge and tip.
Increased width of the columella.
Abnormally decreased lacrimation, that is, reduced ability to produce tears.
Asymmetry of the anterior part of the skull.

A vascular malformation resulting from a developmental error of venous tissue composed of dysmorphic channels lined by flattened endothelium and exhibiting slow turnover. A venous malformation may present as a blue patch on the skin ranging to a soft blue mass. Venous malformations are easily compressible and usually swell in thewhen venous pressure increases (e.g., when held in a dependent position or when a child cries). They may be relatively localized or quite extensive within an anatomic region.
The presence of a notch in the margin of the ala nasi.
An anomaly of cerebral veins.

There is a paramedian frontal encephalocele and a soft tissue cleft that passes medial to an intact eyebrow. The frontal bone shows a paramedian bony cleft with an associated encephalocele. The olfactory groove, cribriform plate, and ethmoid sinus are all increased in transverse diameter, resulting in hypertelorism. The cleft extends medially to the undisturbed eyebrow to end in a short paramedian frontal widow's peak. The bony cleft begins in the region of the nasal bone and extends superiorly through the full height of the frontal bone. Posteriorly, the cleft extends through the cribriform plate and ethmoid sinus as far as the lesser wing and body of the sphenoid. The pterygoid processes are anatomically normal, but they are displaced laterally from the midline on the cleft side. There is orbital hypertelorism below and asymmetry of the floor of the anterior cranial fossa above.

Hyaline membranes are homogeneous eosinophilic material composed of cellular debris, plasma proteins, and surfactant plastered against alveolar ducts and alveolar walls. The hyaline membranes are deposited along the walls of the alveoli, where gas exchange typically occurs, thereby making gas exchange difficult.
Any abnormality of the proximal epiphysis of the femur.
Reduced width of the cross sectional diameter of the fibula.
An increased concentration of insulin in the blood in the fasting state, i.e., not as the response to food intake.
An abnormally elevated concentration of insulin like growth factor binding protein acid labile subunit level in the blood circulation.
Developmental dysplasia of dentin.
Intrapelvic bulging of the medial acetabular wall.
Exaggerated concavity of the anterior or posterior surface of the vertebral body, i.e., the upper and lower vertebral endplates are hollowed inward.
An abnormality of the sclera.

Atherosclerosis which occurs in a person with certain risk factors (e.g., SLE, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, family history of early heart disease) at an earlier age than would occur in another person without those risk factors.
An decreased concentration of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol in the blood.
Limbus-to-limbus corneal thinning, often greatest in the periphery, with globular protrusion of the cornea.
An abnormality of the upper urinary tract.
Absence of one or more interphalangeal creases (i.e., of the transverse lines in the skin between the phalanges of the fingers).
Patellar dislocation occurring repeated times.

A condition in which there is increased production of gastrin by a gastrin-secreting tumor (usually located in the pancreas, duodenum, or abdominal lymph nodes) that stimulates the gastric mucosa to maximal activity, with consequent gastrointestinal mucosal ulceration.
Developmental defect characterized by an anomalous anatomic location of the heart.
Reduced ability to move the femur outward to the side.
A wrinkle of retinal tissue projecting outward from the surface of the retina and visible as a line on fundoscopy.
Camptodactyly is a painless flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint that is usually gradually progressive. This term refers to camptodactyly of one or more toes.
Deficiency of parathyroid hormone with congenital onset.
Hyperexcitability of the neuromuscular system related to abnormally low level of calcium in the blood, resulting in carpopedal or generalized spasms.
The presence of calcium deposition affecting one or more structures of the basal ganglia.
Abnormal thickening of the cortex of the diaphyseal region of long bones.
An abnormality of the medullary cavity (medulla, innermost part), which is the central cavity of bone shafts where red bone marrow and/or yellow bone marrow (adipose tissue) is stored.
Decreased width of the diaphysis of long bones.
Deposition of calcium salts in the retina.
An anomaly of the circulating level of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).
A clonal disorder of keratinization with one or multiple atrophic patches surrounded by a clinically and histologically distinctive hyperkeratotic ridgelike border called the cornoid lamella.
Decreased number of platelet dense granules, a type of platelet organelle.
Loss (disappearance) of previously present subcutaneous fat tissue in arm or leg.
Loss (reduction of previously present) of subcutaneous adipose tissue in the gluteal region.
A reduced circulating concentration of adiponectin, a 30-kDa complement C1-related protein that is the most abundant secreted protein expressed in adipose tissue.
Loss of normal subcutaneous fat tissue in the face.

A structural anomaly of a neuron. Neurons are electrically excitable cells that transmit signals throughout the body. Neurons employ both electrical and chemical components in the transmission of information. Neurons are connected to other neurons at synapses and connected to effector organs or cells at neuroeffector junctions.
DIsruption and breaking up of the basement membrane of the tubules of the kidney.
A type of tremors that is triggered by holding an arm in a fixed position.

A wavering, unsteady voice that reflects involuntary and approximately sinusoidal oscillation of motor unit firings of laryngeal muscles. Vocal tremor results in low frequency modulations of voice frequency or amplitude and intermittent voice instability.
Increased thickness of the stratum corneum (the outer layer of the skin) in the skin surrounding the mouth.
An abnormally increased perspiration on palms and soles.
A clearly-defined and roughly linear cleavage in the skin that usually extends to the dermis.
Tumor of the lung.

A bent (flexed) finger or toe joint that cannot be straightened actively or passively. It is thus a chronic loss of joint motion due to structural changes in muscle, tendons, ligaments, or skin that prevents normal movement of joints.
Toenail changes apart from changes of the color of the toenail (nail dyschromia) that involve partial or complete disruption of the various keratinous layers of the nail plate.
Severe loss of visual acuity within hours or days. This is characteristic of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.
Spontaneous flow of milk from the breast, unassociated with childbirth or nursing.
Abnormally increased concentration of cortisol in the urine.
A reduced ability to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), a hormone that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete of glucocorticoids such as cortisol.
Adrenal insufficiency secondary to a defect in ACTH production.
Episodes of muscle weakness associated with reduced levels of potassium in the blood.
Increased levels of thyroxine without evidence of clinical thyroid disease.
Enlargement of the adrenal gland.
A type of pituitary adenoma that produces adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).

Paralysis of the fourth cranial (trochlear) nerve manifested as weakness of the superior oblique muscle which causes vertical diplopia that is maximal when the affected eye is adducted and directed inferiorly.
Reduced resistance to rupture of capillary blood vessels. Capillary fragility may manifest as a bleeding diathesis with spontaneous ecchymoses (bruises).
Any deviation from the normal sexual drive or desire for sexual activity.
Increased pigmentation, either focal or generalized, of the mucosa of the mouth.
Dminished sexual desire in female.
Paralysis of the iris and ciliary apparatus.
A general descriptive term that describes impaired functioning of the vestibular apparatus that leads to manifestations such as dizziness or postural imbalance
An anomaly of the pituitary gland.
An abnormality of zinc ion homeostasis.
A reduction below the normal concentration of manganese in the blood.

A soft tissue continuity in the anteroposterior axis between adjacent foot digits that involves at least half of the proximodistal length of one of the two involved digits; or, a soft tissue continuity in the A/P axis between two digits of the foot that does not meet the prior objective criteria.
Recurrent bouts of sudden, severe apnea that may be life-threatening.
Decreased activity of complex III of the mitochondrion in the liver.
Inflammation of the iris.
Inflammation of a tendon.
A mode of inheritance that depends on genetic determinants in more than one gene.
Any structural abnormality of the choroid.

Any anomaly of the inflammatory response, a response to injury or infection characterized by local vasodilation, extravasation of plasma into intercellular spaces and accumulation of white blood cells and macrophages.
Any abnormality of the salivary glands, the exocrine glands that produce saliva.
A form of uveitis that is not associated with the formation of granulomas.
A type of vasculitis (inflammation of blood vessel walls) affecting large arteries such as the aorta and branches of the aorta.

Enlargement of the cardiac ventricular muscle tissue with increase in the width of the wall of the ventricle and loss of elasticity. Ventricular hypertrophy is clinically differentiated into left and right ventricular hypertrophy.
A subtype of renal cell carcinoma thought to originate from mature renal tubular cells in the proximal tubule of the nehpron.

Eosinophilic hyaline ovoid bodies which are often found in the subepidermal papillary regions or sometimes in the epidermis. Civatte bodies (CBs) are seen as rounded, homogenous, eosinophilic masses on routine H and E staining lying in the deeper parts of epidermis/epithelium and more frequently in dermis/connective tissue. They are known as CBs (in epithelium/epidermis), colloid bodies, or hyaline bodies (in connective tissue). They are 10-25 micrometers in diameter and situated mostly within or above the inflammatory cell infiltrate. In lichen planus, the number of necrotic keratinocytes may be so large that they are seen lying in clusters in the uppermost dermis. These bodies show a positive periodic acid Schiff reaction and are diastase resistant

Irregular lines in the deep retina that are typically configured in a radiating fashion and emanate from the optic disc. Angioid streaks are crack-like dehiscences in abnormally thickened and calcified Bruch's membrane, resulting in atrophy of the overlying retinal pigment epithelium. They may be associated with a number of endocrine, metabolic, and connective tissue abnormalities but are frequently idiopathic.
Abnormal thinning of the cortical region of bones.
A diminution in the amplitude (strength) of the pulse such that the examiner has difficulty feeling the pulse.
A break or crush injury of the thigh bone (femur).
Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is the creation of new blood vessels in the choroid layer of the eye.
A small circumscribed whitish change in the color of the oral mucosa that is neither elevated nor depressed.
A pebbly orange appearance of the fundus that is said to resemble the skin of an orange.
Absence or underdevelopment of the lens.
A papule with yellow color.
A congenital malformation of the aortic valve characterized by leaflet deformation.

Restrictive left ventricular physiology is characterized by a pattern of ventricular filling in which increased stiffness of the myocardium causes ventricular pressure to rise precipitously with only small increases in volume, defined as restrictive ventricular physiology in the presence of normal or reduced diastolic volumes (of one or both ventricles), normal or reduced systolic volumes, and normal ventricular wall thickness.
An abnormally increased concentration of the IgG3 subtype in the blood circulation.
The presence of calcium deposition in the cerebral white matter surrounding the cerebral ventricles.
Developmental hypoplasia of the tooth germ, i.e., of the structure that forms in odontogenesis that will develop into a tooth.
Tooth root length more than 2 SD below mean, or subjectively apparently decreased tooth root length.
A generalized form of lymphadenopathy.
Breakage (tear) of a tendon.
An increased susceptibility to viral upper respiratory tract infections as manifested by a history of recurrent viral upper respiratory tract infections (otitis, sinusitis, pharyngitis, tonsillitis).
Increased susceptibility to viral pneumonia, as manifested by recurrent episodes of viral pneumonias.
The vomiting of blood.
Increased concentration of interferon alpha in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

Chilblains, also called perniosis, are an inflammatory skin condition related to an abnormal vascular response to the cold. We are unaware of a reliable estimate of incidence. It typically presents as tender, pruritic red or bluish lesions located symmetrically on the dorsal aspect of the fingers, toes, ears and nose. Less commonly, reports describe involvement of the thighs and buttocks. The lesions present hours after exposure to cold and usually resolve spontaneously in one to three weeks.
Chronic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lymphocytosis is defined as the finding, in at least two serial CSF examinations, of more than 5 cells per cubic millimeter.
Low platelet count associated with maternal platelet-specific alloantibodies.
Muscular rigidity (continuous contraction of muscles with constant resistance to passive movement).
Bluish discoloration of the skin of the hands or feet.
A reduction in immunoglobulin levels of the IgG3 subclass in the blood circulation.
Abnormal calcification of the mitral valve.
A tooth which does not erupt within the teeth eruption timeline and after the loss of eruption potential.
Underdevelopment of the distal epiphysis of the radius.
Calcification, that is, pathological deposition of calcium salts in the arch of aorta.
Detachment of the nail from the nail bed.

The term tinea means fungal infection, whereas dermatophyte refers to the fungal organisms that cause tinea. This term refers to a tinea infection that is chronic or recalcitrant to treatment and may be reflective of an immune defect.
A type of invasive dermatophyte infection of the deep dermis characterized by extensive dermal infiltration by fungal elements.
A severely increased count of eosinophils in the blood defined as a blood eosinophil count of at least 1.5 billion cells per liter.
Any abnormality in the proportion of CD4-positive T cells relative to the total number of T cells.
Any abnormality in the proportion of CD8 T cells relative to the total number of T cells.
A fungal infection of the toenails or fingernails that tends to cause the nails to thicken, discolor, disfigure, and split.
An abnormal backward rotation of the hip relative to the knee such that the hips are externally rotated with the foot pointed outward instead of straight ahead (out-toeing).
A cancer arising in any part of the stomach.

A deviation from the normal concentration of creatine in the blood circulation. Creatine is a derivative of glycine having methyl and amidino groups attached to the nitrogen. Creatine is naturally produced from amino acids, primarily in liver and kidney, and acts as an energy source for cells, primarly for muscle cells.
The presence of a neoplasm of the kidney.
A tumor (abnormal growth of tissue) of the uterus.
Any anomaly of the structure of the spleen.
Any structural anomaly of the lung.

A developmental defect of the alveolar airspace during cananicular lung development characterized by a decreased number of pulmonary capillaries located away from the alveolar epithelium, thickened alveolar septae, media hypertrophy of small pulmonary arteries and muscularization of distal arterioles, and in some cases lymphangiectasis.

The fetal spleen is lobulated, and these lobules normally disappear before the birth. Lobulation of the spleen may persist into adult life and be typically seen along the medial part of the spleen. A persisting lobule results in a variation in shape of the spleen.
A congenital failure of muscular development of part or all of one or both hemidiaphragms, resulting in superior displacement of abdominal viscera and altered lung development.
Underdeveloped, small left heart atrium
A developmental defect characterized by the lack of formation of the pulmonary blood vessels.

A supranuclear gaze palsy is an inability to look in a horizontal direction as a result of cerebral impairment. There is a loss of the voluntary aspect of eye movements, but, as the brainstem is still intact, all the reflex conjugate eye movements are normal.
An increased concentration of beta-sitosterol in the blood circulation.
The presence of xanthomata in the skin of the eyelid.
A type of xanthoma characterized by a nodular form. Tuberous xanthomas are firm subcutaneous nodules,whereby the overlying skin can have red or red-yellow color changes.
Hyperapobetalipoproteinemia is defined as the combination of a normal low density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol in the face of an increased LDL apolipoprotein B (apoB) protein.
An chronic form of hemolytic anemia.

An impairment in the rate and degree to which platelets aggregate after the addition of an agonist that stimulates platelet clumping. Platelet aggregation is measured using aggregometer to measure the optical density of platelet-rich plasma, whereby platelet aggregation causes the plasma to become more transparent.
A form of hemolytic anemia that occurs in repeated episodes.

An abnormally low concentration of haptoglobin in the blood circulation. Decreased haptoglobin in conjunction with increased reticulocyte count and anemia may indicate hemolysis. Decreased haptoglobin levels can also occur in the absence of hemolysis, due to cirrhosis of the liver, disseminated ovarian carcinomatosis, pulmonary sarcoidosis, and elevated estrogen state.

Giant platelets are larger than 7 micrometers and usually 10 to 20 micrometers. The term giant platelet is used when the platelet is larger than the size of the average red cell in the field. (Description adapted from College of American Pathologists, Hematology Manual, 1998).
The presence of erythrocytes with a mouth-shaped (stoma) area of central pallor on peripheral blood smear.
Vesicoureteral reflux with dilatation of the collecting system.
Vesicoureteral reflux with more-extensive dilation with blunting of the calyces and tortuosity of the ureter.
A complete duplication of the ureter, where the duplicated ureters have separate insertions into the bladder.
Increased length of multiple or a single phalanx of finger.
An abnormally increased length of the metacarpal bones.

Bigonial distance (lower facial width) more than 2 standard deviations below the mean (objective); or an apparently decreased width of the lower jaw (mandible) when viewed from the front (subjective).
Missing ulna bone associated with congenital failure of development.
Reduced distance from the anterior border of the naris to the subnasale.
Congenital duplication of all or part of a limb.
The presence of more than the normal number of metacarpal bones.
Displacement of the hand or of fingers of the hand from their normal position.
Complete duplication of the distal phalanx of the thumb. On x-ray two separate bones appear side to side.
Complete duplication of the distal phalanx of the thumb. On x-ray two separate bones appear side to side.
Duplication of the fibula. This may occur as a part of diplopodia (accessory tarsal or metatarsal bone). Diplopodia with double fibula is an extremely rare condition.
Syndactyly with fusion of fingers one to five (complete syndactyly of all fingers of the hand).

A hand or foot with more than five digits that has a recognizable A/P axis of symmetry. The axis can lie within a normally formed or partially duplicated digit resembling a middle finger, index finger, thumb, toe, or hallux. Alternatively, the axis can be in an interdigital space with a flanking pair of digits that resemble a middle finger, index finger, thumb, toe or hallux. The most lateral digits on each side of the hand/foot typically resemble fifth fingers/toes.
Synostosis (bony fusion) involving one or more bones of the tarsus (calcaneus, talus, cuboid, navicular, cuneiiform bones).
The distal parts of the limbs are missing leading to a stump formation.
Peromelia affecting only the lower limbs. That is, the distal parts of the leg are missing leading to stump formation.

Missing or malformed long bones of the upper limbs with the distal parts (the hands) connected to the variably shortened or even absent upper extremity, leading to a flipper-like appearance, as opposed to other forms of limb malformations were either the whole limb is missing (such as amelia), or the distal part of a limb is absent (peromelia).
Absence of one or more of the phalanges of the hand.
A developmental abnormality characterized by the absence (aplasia) of a metatarsal bone.
An anomaly of trapezium.
Congenital absence of a carpal bone.
A form of triphalangeal thumb that can be placed opposite the fingers of the same hand.
An anomaly of the calf bone (fibula), one of the two bones of the calf.
Absence of the fibula.
Underdevelopment of part or all of the female external reproductive organs (which include the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, Bartholin glands, and clitoris).
Lack of the uvula.
Exaggerated convexity of the cervical vertebral column, causing the cervical spine to bow outwards and take on a rounded appearance.

An abnormality of the hand characterized by metacarpophalangeal (MCP) hyperextension and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) flexion. The position of the affected hand is said to resemble a claw.

A failure to achieve the ability to crawl at an appropriate developmental stage. Normal infant motor development is marked by a series of postural milestones including learning to crawl on hands and knees between the ages of 6 and 10 months.
Delayed ahcievement of the ability to roll front to back and back to front.
Recurrent infection involving the vulva, vagina, and adjacent crural areas, whereby the causative agent belongs to the genus Candida.
A type of dystonia (abnormally increased muscular tone causing fixed abnormal postures) that affects muscles of the legs.
Hyperkeratosis affecting the sole of the foot.

An abnormal union between bones or parts of bones of the fingers. The synonymous term "symphalangism of the hand" may be translated as fusions of bones of varying digree, that involve at least one phalangeal bone of the hand. If bony fusions are referred to as "Symphalangism" the fusion occurs in a proximo-distal axis. Fusions of bones of the fingers in a radio-ulnar axis are referred to as "bony" Syndactyly.
Abnormal structure or form of trabecular bone.
A partial or complete breakage of the continuity of a bone.
Abnormal functionality of the gastrointestinal tract.
An abnormal accumulation of fluid and swelling in the tissues of the larynx.
An abnormal accumulation of fluid beneath the skin on the back of the hands.
Ultra-low vision but with retained ability to perceive the difference between light and dark.
Repetitive pressing, poking, and/or rubbing in the eyes.
Scar tissue in the macula.
Best corrected visual acuity worse than 1.90 logMAR (roughly 20/1590).
Separation of the odontoid process from the body of the axis.

An abnormality of the auditory evoked potentials, which are used to trace the signal generated by a sound, from the cochlear nerve, through the lateral lemniscus, to the medial geniculate nucleus, and to the cortex.

Sharply demarcated area of partial or complete depigmentation of the fundus reflecting atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium with associated retinal photoreceptor loss. The margins of the de-pigmented area are usually scalloped and the large choroidal vessels are visible through the atrophic retinal pigment epithelium.
Decreased amount of pigmentation in the macula lutea.
Abnormal platelet response to ADP as manifested by reduced or lacking aggregation of platelets upon addition of ADP.
Bleeding that persists longer than the normal time following a surgical procedure.
Syndactyly with fusion of fingers three and four.
Difference in length or size between the right and left arm.
A bone tumor composed of cellular spindle-cell stroma containing scattered multinucleated giant cells resembling osteoclasts.

A lamellar pattern visible on radiographs and mainly localized at the metaphyses of the long tubular bones. Pathologic-anatomical studies revealed that these benign signs on x-rays are the result of a juvenile metaphyseal bone necrosis. Calcifications in the necrotic marrow lead to this lamellar or lattice-like appearance.
A tumor of the skin or mucous membrane with finger-like projections.
An abnormality of adipose tissue, which is loose connective tissue composed of adipocytes.
A wart-like lesion (papilloma, i.e., benign epithelial tumors that are caused by infection with the human papilloma virus) located on the larynx.
Incomplete duplication of the ureter.
Underdevelopment of the middle portion of the clavicle.
Developmental defect resulting in congenital absence of the middle portion of the clavicle.
Congenital absence of the toenail.
The presence of two to five cafe-au-lait macules.
Unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment.

Reduced level of T cell receptor excision circle (TRECs) as measured by the TREC assay. Late in maturation, 70% of thymocytes that will ultimately express alpha/beta-T cell receptors form a circular DNA TREC from the excised TCRdelta gene that lies within the TCRalpha genetic locus. The circles are stable but do not increase following cell division and, therefore, become diluted as T cells proliferate. A quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) reaction across the joint of the circular DNA provides the TREC copy number, a marker of newly-formed, antigenically-naïve thymic emigrant T cells.
An abnormality of the optic nerve in which the optic nerve is large and funneled and displays a conical excavation of the optic disc. The optic disc appears dysplastic.
An increased concentration of heparan sulfates in the urine.
Excretion of glycosaminoglycan in the urine. Glycosaminoglycans are long unbranched polysaccharides consisting of a repeating disaccharide unit.
Severely increased levels of protein in the urine (1000-3000 mg per day in adults).
For children from birth to 16 years of age the length of the palm is more than the 97th centile; or, the length of the palm appears relatively long compared to the finger length or the limb length.
An increased tendency to fractures following trauma, with fractures occurring without pain.
An decreased level of renin in the blood.
An abnormal reduction of the concentration of bicarbonate, HCO3[-], in the circulation.
The presence of misshapen or partially destroyed nail plates, often with accumulation of soft, yellow keratin between the dystrophic nail plate and nail bed, resulting in elevation of the nail plate.

An abnormally reduced response to stimulation of the cornea (by touch, foreign body, blowing air). The corneal reflex (also known as the blink reflex, normally results in an involuntary blinking of the eyelids.
A herniation of meninges through a congenital bone defect in the skull in the occipital region.
A subtle unilateral cleft of the upper lip, which may appear as a small indentation.
A structural abnormality of the retina.
Any structural anomaly of the bronchi, i.e., of the airways leading from the trachea to the lungs.
A kind of short stature in which different regions of the body are shortened to differing extents.
Relatively increased growth of the fibula compared to that of the tibia.
A generalized decrease in bone mineral density.
A bending or abnormal curvature affecting a long bone of the leg.
A benign or malignant neoplasm that occurs within the intracranial cavity above the tentorium cerebelli.

A limitation of the ability to place the forearm in a position such that the palm faces anteriorly (supination) and to place the forearm in a position such that the palm faces posteriorly (pronation).
Failure to form of portions of the abdominal musculature.
Abnormality of the anterior chamber, which is the space in the eye that is behind the cornea and in front of the iris.

Reduced activity of coagulation factor VII. Factor VII is part of the extrinsic coagulation pathway, which is initiated at the site of injury in response to the release of tissue factor (fIII). Tissue factor and activated factor VII catalyze the activation of factor X.
Decreased activity of coagulation factor IX. Factor IX, which itself is activated by factor Xa or factor VIIa to form factor IXa, activates factor X into factor Xa.

Reduced activity of coagulation factor X. The extrinsic and intrinsic pathways converge at factor X (fX). The extrinsic pathway activates fX by means of d factor VII with its cofactor, tissue factor. The intrinsic pathway activates fX by means of the tenase complex (Ca2+ and factors VIIIa, IXa and X) on the surface of activated platelets. Factor Xa in turn activates prothrombin (factor II) to thrombin (factor IIa).
Reduced prothrombin antigen as measured by ELISA assay. Prothrombin is a vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor that is proteolytically cleaved to form thrombin.
A reduced concentration of free 3,3',5-triiodo-L-thyronine in the blood circulation.
Any deviation from the normal circulating concentration of selenium.
An elevated concentration of free thyroxine (fT4) in the blood circulation.

An elevation above the normal concentration of thyroxine in the blood. Thyroxine (also known as T4) is the main hormone secreted by the thyroid gland into the blood. It can be converted into the active form triiodothyronine (also known as T3).
The presence of an increased degree of wrinkling (irregular folds and indentations) of the skin as compared with age-related norms.

A type of soft tissue sarcoma with a histological appearance reminiscent of alveoli because of its reticulated fibrous stroma enclosing groups of sarcoma cells, which resemble epithelial cells and are enclosed in alveoli walled with connective tissue.
Rounding and broadening of the tufts of the distal phalanges.
Increased width of the alveolar ridges.
White color (lack of pigmentation) of the eyelashes.
An abnormal deviation from normal levels of IgG immunoglobulin in blood.
An abnormal deviation from normal levels of IgM immunoglobulin in blood.
An abnormal deviation from normal levels of IgA immunoglobulin in blood.
Increased susceptibility to ear infections, as manifested by recurrent episodes of ear infections.

A structural abnormality of the peripheral nervous system, which is composed of the nerves that lead to or branch off from the central nervous system. This includes the cranial nerves (olfactory and optic nerves are technically part of the central nervous system).
An increase in size of the anatomic space between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater in the region surrounding the cerebrum.
Thickening and hardening of the epidermis seen with exaggeration of normal skin lines.
A thickening of the stratum corneum in the region beneath the nails.

An anomaly of the hair follicles of the skin that typically presents as small, rough, brown folliculocentric papules distributed over characteristic areas of the skin, particularly the outer-upper arms and thighs.
Congenital absence of the left half of the diaphragm.

The presence, on T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging, of markedly low signal intensity of the globus pallidus that surrounds a central region of high signal intensity in the anteromedial globus pallidus, producing an eye-of-the-tiger appearance. The sign is thought to represent iron accumulation in the globus pallidus.
Increased frequency of urination.
A tachycardia originating in the ventricles characterized by rapid heart rate (over 100 beats per minute) and broad QRS complexes (over 120 ms).

A type of hearing impairment prominently characterized by a difficulty in understanding speech, rather than an inability to hear speech. Poor speech discrimination is a very common symptom of high frequency hearing loss.
Presyncope is a state of lightheadedness, muscular weakness, blurred vision, and feeling faint. Presyncope is most often cardiovascular in cause.
Right ventricular dysfunction (global or regional) with functional and morphological right ventricular abnormalities, with or without left ventricular disease.
Pattern of blood flow in the heart that deviates from the normal circuit of the circulatory system from the left side of the heart to the right.
The growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus.
A compact, organized collection of mature mononuclear phagocytes, which may be but is not necessarily accompanied by accessory features such as necrosis.
The presence of an abscess located around the anus.

In the NBT test, neutrophils change the colorless compound NBT into a compound with a deep blue color. If this test is negative (i.e., no blue color is produced), then this indicates a defect in superoxide-generating NADPH oxidase activity with inability to efficiently kill phagocytized bacteria.
Inflammation of a lymph node.
A small tear in the thin, moist tissue (mucosa) that lines the anus. It appears as a crack or slit in the mucous membrane of the anus.

Inflammation of the tonsils that has occurred repeatedly. The definition of recurrent may vary somewhat, but the criteria used recently as a measure of severity were five or more episodes of true tonsillitis per year, symptoms recurring for at least a year, and episodes that are disabling and that prevent normal functioning. In some cases recurrent tonsillitis may be related to immunosusceptibility. Evidence exists for a genetic predisposition for recurrent tonsillitis.
A disordered proliferation of mature tissues that are native to the kidneys.
A structural abnormality of the parathyroid gland.
A type of hyperparathyroidism caused by a primary abnormality of the parathyroid glands (e.g., adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia). Primary hyperparathyroidism is associated with hyercalcemia.

Benign tumors that are composed of fibrous or connective tissue. They can grow in all organs, arising from mesenchyme tissue. The term "fibroblastic" or "fibromatous" is used to describe tumors of the fibrous connective tissue. When the term fibroma is used without modifier, it is usually considered benign, with the term fibrosarcoma reserved for malignant tumors.
An unpleasant sensation characterized by physical discomfort (such as pricking, throbbing, or aching) localized to the mandible.
A subjective manifestation of disease localized to the abdomen.
An increased excretion of phosphates in the urine.
Decreased time between the start of the Q wave and the end of the T wave as measured by the electrocardiogram (EKG).
A benign tumor of the parathyroid gland that can cause hyperparathyroidism.
The presence of an adenoma in the cortex of the kidney.
A malignancy of the parathyroid glands. Parathyroid carcinoma usually secretes parathyroid hormone, leading to hyperparathyroidism.
A kind of thyroid adenoma characterized by the presence of oxyphil cells.
The presence of renal cell carcinoma in the renal papilla.

Seesaw nystagmus is a type of pendular nystagmus where a half cycle consists of the elevation and intorsion of one eye, concurrently with the depression and extortion of the fellow eye. In the other half cycle, there is an inversion of the ocular movements.
Pallor of the perifoveal macula of the retina with appearance of a small circular reddish choroid shape as seen through the fovea centralis due to relative transparancy of the macula.
Focal seizure with eyelid myoclonia, not eyelid myoclonias in the context of absence seizures.

An arachnoid cyst that progressively enlarges from an abnormality in the membrane of Liliequist or in the interpeduncular cistern, and typically, expands from the prepontine space, displacing the floor of the third ventricle upwards, the pituitary stalk and optic chiasm upwards and forwards, and the mammillary bodies upwards and backwards.
Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges (PLEDs)are periodic, lateralized, and epileptiform. PLEDs show a relatively constant interval between discharges (0.5 to 3 seconds).
Angiectasia of lymph vessels (i.e., dilatation of lymphatic vessels) in the intestines.

A form of subcortical heterotopia with mislocalized gray matter within the white matter.It is defined as longitudinal bands of gray matter located deep to the cerebral cortex and separated from it by a thin layer of normal appearing white matter. It is part of the lissencephaly spectrum.
A structural anomaly of the trachea.

Lymphangiomas are rare congenital malformations consisting of focal proliferations of well-differentiated lymphatic tissue in multi cystic or sponge like structures. Lymphangioma is usually asymptomatic due to its soft consistency but compression of adjacent structures can be seen due to the mass effect of a large tumor.
Increased susceptibility to erysipelas, as manifested by a medical history of repeated episodes of erysipelas, which is a superficial infection of the skin, typically involving the lymphatic system.
Accumulation of excessive amounts of lymphatic fluid (chyle) in the pleural cavity.
An abnormal dilatation of lymph vessels in the pericardium.
An increased rate of premature chromosome condensation.
Any physiological abnormality of the esophagus.
